content: HIV testing services (HTS) should be integrated into all epidemic settings, especially in areas with a high burden of HIV. Decentralization of HTS involves providing testing services at peripheral health facilities, such as primary healthcare centers, or even outside formal health facilities within the community. This approach can reduce transportation costs, waiting times, and other barriers associated with accessing central hospitals, thereby improving accessibility and uptake of testing services. However, decentralization may not always be appropriate or resource-efficient, particularly in low HIV burden settings or where stigma and discrimination deter key populations from seeking services. Careful consideration of the local context, service gaps, costs, and community preferences is essential when deciding on decentralization. Strengthening referral and linkage systems is critical to ensure the success of decentralized services. Task sharing in HTS involves redistributing responsibilities between healthcare providers with varying levels of training, including trained lay providers. Lay providers, such as community health workers or trained peers, can deliver HTS using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). This approach enhances accessibility, acceptability, and service delivery, particularly in underserved areas. Lay providers can also offer a range of health services beyond HIV testing, such as TB, viral hepatitis, and STI screening, as well as sexual and reproductive health services. WHO strongly recommends the use of trained and supervised lay providers to independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing services. The test for triage strategy involves a trained provider performing a single HIV RDT and linking individuals with reactive results to further confirmatory testing and appropriate services. This approach supports the role of lay providers and expands community-based HTS. Similarly, HIV self-testing (HIVST) allows individuals to perform a self-test and seek confirmatory testing if the result is reactive. Both strategies aim to improve early diagnosis and linkage to care. Facility-based HTS includes testing in health facilities or laboratories, either at stand-alone sites (e.g., voluntary counseling and testing centers) or as part of routine clinical services (e.g., provider-initiated testing and counseling). Routine facility-based HTS is particularly effective in high HIV burden settings, where it can be offered to all clients attending clinical services. In low HIV burden settings, HTS should focus on key populations, individuals with HIV indicator conditions, and clients in specific clinical settings such as TB, STI, or antenatal care (ANC) clinics. Routine HTS aims to normalize testing, increase coverage, and reduce missed opportunities for diagnosis. Integration of HTS into ANC services has been highly successful in high HIV burden settings, contributing to high testing coverage among pregnant women. WHO recommends routine HTS for all pregnant women, along with testing for syphilis and hepatitis B, using dual HIV/syphilis RDTs where available. This approach is cost-saving and helps eliminate adverse birth outcomes due to syphilis. However, integration of HTS into ANC services remains less effective in low HIV burden settings. Contraception and family planning services provide an opportunity to integrate HTS as part of sexual and reproductive health packages, particularly for adolescent girls, young women, and their partners in high HIV burden settings. This integration addresses the diverse needs of sexually active adolescents and helps prevent HIV transmission. HTS should also be routinely offered to infants and children with unknown HIV status who are admitted for inpatient care or attending outpatient, malnutrition, or immunization clinics in high HIV burden settings. Testing of HIV-exposed or sick children remains a key strategy for identifying additional HIV infections. TB services provide a critical entry point for HTS, as TB is a leading cause of death among people with HIV. Routine HTS should be offered to all clients with presumptive or confirmed TB, and intensified TB case finding should be conducted among people with HIV. Early detection and prompt linkage to TB treatment and antiretroviral therapy (ART) can prevent deaths among people with HIV. Clinical and prevention services for key populations, such as harm reduction services for people who inject drugs and clinical services in prisons, should prioritize HTS to minimize missed opportunities for diagnosis. Similarly, STI clinics provide an important entry point for HTS, as HIV and STI co-infection is common. Routine HTS should be offered to all individuals with STIs. Integration of HTS into viral hepatitis services should be prioritized for populations most affected by both HIV and hepatitis, such as people who inject drugs and prison populations. Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) services in high HIV burden countries also include HTS as part of service delivery, with high uptake among men. Structural and policy barriers, such as stockouts of test kits and age of consent laws, need to be addressed to facilitate effective HTS integration. In hospital settings, HTS should be offered in inpatient, outpatient, and emergency services to clients with symptoms or conditions indicative of HIV infection. Risk-based screening tools may help identify individuals for testing in low HIV burden settings or where HTS is not readily available. These tools should be validated and implemented with input from affected populations.
